title: CROSS JOIN & Cartesian Products
description: Generate Cartesian products, create matrix combinations (sizes x colors), and avoid accidental performance catastrophes.

data.text: A **`CROSS JOIN`** produces the Cartesian product of two tables. Every row from Table A is paired with every row from Table B. If Table A contains 10 rows and Table B contains 50 rows, the resulting table contains exactly 10 × 50 = 500 rows.
Practical Use: Generating Product Variant SKUs

data.title: Generating All Size and Color Combinations
data.content: Permuting attributes to generate inventory SKU matrices.
data.code:
SELECT 
    p.name AS product_name,
    s.size_label,
    c.color_name,
    CONCAT(p.code, '-', s.size_code, '-', c.color_code) AS generated_sku
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c
WHERE p.is_active = true;

data.title: Accidental Cartesian Explosion
data.text: Never omit the `ON` condition in an old-style comma join (`FROM table_a, table_b`)! If Table A has 100,000 rows and Table B has 100,000 rows, an accidental CROSS JOIN computes 10,000,000,000 rows, exhausting database memory and crashing production!
When a CROSS JOIN Is the Right Tool

A Cartesian product is a bug when it happens by accident, but it is exactly what you want when you need every combination of two sets. The most common legitimate use is a date spine: pair every day in a range with every store, product, or customer, then left join the facts. Rows with no activity appear with `NULL` or zero instead of vanishing, which makes trend charts and gap-filling reports correct.

data.title: Building a date spine and filling gaps
data.content: `generate_series` produces the days, and a LEFT JOIN attaches whatever sales exist. Stores with no sales that day still appear with zero.
data.code:
WITH days AS (
    SELECT day::date AS sales_day
    FROM generate_series(
        DATE '2024-01-01',
        DATE '2024-01-31',
        INTERVAL '1 day'
    ) AS day
),
stores AS (
    SELECT id, name FROM stores
)
SELECT
    s.name            AS store_name,
    d.sales_day,
    COALESCE(SUM(sa.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM days AS d
CROSS JOIN stores AS s
LEFT JOIN sales AS sa
    ON sa.store_id = s.id
   AND sa.sold_on = d.sales_day
GROUP BY s.name, d.sales_day
ORDER BY d.sales_day, s.name;

data.title: Interview angle: prove you know the difference
data.text: Interviewers use CROSS JOIN to test whether you understand cardinality. Say the size of the result explicitly: a 1,000-row set cross joined with a 100-row set yields 100,000 rows before any filter. Then say when it is intentional (date spines, permutations, SKU matrices) and how you keep it bounded (filter both sides first, and never put a CROSS JOIN under an accidental missing predicate).

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `CROSS JOIN` multiplies the cardinality of both tables (M × N).
Useful for calendar day filling, permutations, and SKU matrix generation.
Always use explicit `CROSS JOIN` syntax rather than comma joins.
